=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s position

**Do not accept the package as settled.** The Seller’s “[STANDARD]” labels and reviewer note are not evidence of Buyer agreement. They cannot substitute for substantive review.

The central problem is the interaction between **blanket disclosure, deemed Buyer knowledge and limitations applying to “all Claims”**. Together, these could leave Wattlebridge accepting known risks while also losing the contractual remedies intended to address them.

This review is based on the Seller’s update and Disclosure Letter—not the full SPA or underlying DD documents. References to those documents should be verified before agreeing drafting.

## Material issues and proposed pushback

### 1. The limitations could undermine the entire protection package

**Seller position:** A 20% general warranty cap—AUD 4.8 million—plus AUD 25,000 de minimis, AUD 250,000 deductible basket and 18-month notification period. Limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance extend to all Claims unless expressly excluded.

**Buyer concern:** The general warranty figures are negotiable commercial terms, not automatically acceptable because labelled “standard”. More importantly, the broad language could capture title, tax, specific indemnities, completion obligations and price-adjustment claims. A separately negotiated indemnity may be ineffective if caught by the same cap, basket, time limit or disclosure defence.

**Push back:**
- Establish an express hierarchy separating general warranties, fundamental warranties, tax claims, specific indemnities, price adjustments and other contractual obligations.
- Limit the general warranty regime to its intended category, with consistent carve-outs throughout clauses 9.3, 12, 13 and 20.5.
- Preserve claims for fraud and fraudulent concealment and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded; review the reach and enforceability of non-reliance and exclusive-remedy wording under NSW law.
- Seek a higher general cap, lower thresholds and a **tipping basket**—once crossed, qualifying losses are recoverable from the first dollar, rather than only the excess.
- Aggregate related claims for threshold purposes so a common issue cannot be fragmented below the de minimis.
- Seek a longer general warranty period, preferably covering two full reporting cycles. Check notice requirements and any subsequent proceedings deadline so properly notified claims survive.

### 2. Fundamental warranties should not receive ordinary warranty protection

**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties receive the same cap and time limits as general warranties.

**Buyer concern:** Wattlebridge is paying AUD 24 million for valid ownership of all shares. A maximum AUD 4.8 million recovery, expiring after 18 months, is inadequate if the Seller lacked authority or did not deliver the agreed ownership.

**Push back:** Require separate fundamental warranties covering capacity, authority, ownership, valid issue, the entire issued capital and absence of encumbrances or third-party rights. Seek protection up to at least the full purchase price, without general warranty thresholds, and a substantially longer claim period.

DD-012 is useful evidence, **not conclusive verification of the whole title position**. Check the register against supporting issue and transfer records, the constitution, shareholder arrangements and relevant security searches; require appropriate transfer documents and releases at Completion.

### 3. Blanket disclosure and deemed knowledge transfer too much risk

**Seller position:** Everything contained or referred to in the data room, accounts, registers and public records is generally disclosed. Anything the Buyer or advisers knew—or could discover—bars claims.

**Buyer concern:** This converts access to information into acceptance of its legal and financial consequences. It also imports potentially extensive adviser knowledge and constructive knowledge. A buried document or incomplete reference could defeat a warranty.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure in sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**, preferably against the relevant warranty.
- Reject unrestricted disclosure of public records, referenced materials and the entire data room.
- Preserve a fixed, indexed copy of the disclosed materials and control late updates.
- Delete the constructive-knowledge test. If a knowledge exclusion is conceded, confine it to actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel, with no general adviser imputation or duty of inquiry.
- State expressly that disclosure and Buyer knowledge do **not** qualify agreed specific indemnities, completion requirements or price adjustments.

The Disclosure Letter’s caveat that it admits no liability does not resolve the underlying risks.

### 4. Bluefen: obtaining a letter is not enough

**Facts disclosed:** Approximately AUD 3.6 million revenue, around 30% of FY26 revenue; change-control conditions in clause 11.3; no final consent or evidence of satisfaction.

**Buyer concern:** This is a major revenue dependency. “Reasonable endeavours” is an effort obligation, not a guaranteed outcome. A written consent may still contain unsatisfied conditions or commercially damaging changes.

**Push back:** Make effective Bluefen consent a genuine condition precedent, waivable only by the Buyer. Require review of the complete consent and satisfaction of associated conditions, with no unacceptable amendments, fees or adverse commercial terms. Include a long-stop date and appropriate termination rights.

**Do not deem the condition satisfied merely because a consent document is delivered.**

### 5. Riverlark: discharge must be coordinated with Completion

**Facts disclosed:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million outstanding; facility not repaid; no final security discharge.

**Buyer concern:** A post-Completion promise leaves the acquired company exposed to debt, security enforcement and potential change-control consequences. It conflicts with the debt-free/cash-free bargain unless properly addressed.

**Push back:**
- Obtain an agreed payoff statement including accrued interest, fees and break costs.
- Arrange repayment through the Completion funds flow, with binding release arrangements and the required discharge documents and registrations.
- Make delivery of satisfactory repayment and release arrangements a Completion requirement.
- Ensure the purchase-price bridge treats the debt consistently: **no residual debt and no double counting** between the equity-price adjustment and repayment allocation.

### 6. Completion bonuses: ensure the Seller actually bears the cost

**Facts disclosed:** AUD 420,000 of conditional Completion bonuses omitted from the draft funds flow; on-costs unspecified.

**Buyer concern:** Calling these “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the target from becoming liable after Completion, leaving the Buyer to fund them.

**Push back:** Confirm the recipients, conditions, payment timing and all applicable superannuation, payroll tax, withholding and other costs. Allocate the agreed Seller-borne liability through a specific price deduction, debt-like adjustment or funded payment mechanism, backed by an indemnity for residual exposure. Avoid counting it twice through working capital and a separate deduction.

### 7. Ironquay: payment exposure and IP ownership are different risks

**Facts disclosed:** SOW3 transfer depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee; AUD 180,000 recorded as open; no receipt or confirmatory assignment.

**Buyer concern:** The records do not conclusively prove non-payment, but neither do they establish that title transferred. An indemnity limited to a particular invoice may fail to cover loss arising from missing IP rights.

**Push back:**
- Reconcile all relevant SOW3 fees and obtain evidence of cleared payment.
- Obtain an effective confirmatory assignment and verify the rights necessary to use, modify and commercialise the relevant materials.
- Where the materials are critical, require resolution before Completion.
- Expand the specific indemnity to cover the identified ownership defect and resulting remediation, replacement, infringement and business losses, subject to carefully negotiated scope—not merely the AUD 180,000 payment.
- Check the wider IP chain of title rather than treating this payment as proof that all IP warranties are settled.

### 8. Export/privacy incident: investigate without overstating the evidence

**Facts disclosed:** A download link went to an unintended external address; potentially around 1,240 records; access, scope and notification requirements remain uncertain.

**Buyer concern:** The Seller’s “not expected to be material” characterisation is unsupported. Equally, the evidence does **not** establish a confirmed notifiable breach or quantify loss.

**Push back:**
- Require prompt investigation, preservation of logs, containment and evidence about access, link controls, recipients, affected information and contractual obligations.
- Assess applicable privacy, breach-notification and customer-notification requirements on the findings.
- Require pre-Completion updates and consultation on material communications, without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-Completion incident and associated investigation, remediation and third-party exposure, with appropriate scope and enforceability qualifications.
- Consider a retention or escrow if uncertainty remains material at Completion.

Do not let disclosure alone extinguish the remedy for this known, unresolved issue.

### 9. Sandbar renewals: assess the aggregate commitment

**Facts disclosed:** Three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each—AUD 330,000 in total. Their timing and scope must be read together.

**Buyer concern:** Splitting related commitments may conceal their significance under interim operating covenants or approval thresholds. “Ordinary course” is not established merely by assertion.

**Push back:** Review them together for term, termination rights, necessity, pricing, accrual and timing. Apply related-transaction aggregation to consent thresholds. Determine whether they affect working capital, debt-like items or a covenant breach.

**Do not automatically deduct AUD 330,000 from price:** genuine future operating expenditure is not necessarily Seller debt.

### 10. Tax needs separate treatment; IP needs targeted protection

**Buyer concern:** An 18-month, 20%-capped general warranty regime may provide little protection against historic tax liabilities discovered later. IP defects may likewise emerge after integration.

**Push back:** Seek a separate tax covenant or indemnity allocating pre-Completion tax to the Seller, with appropriately longer survival, tailored limitations and conduct-of-claims provisions. Review exclusions and accounting provisions to prevent gaps or double recovery.

For IP, require substantive ownership, licensing and infringement warranties and appropriate survival and caps, alongside the specific Ironquay solution. Neither area is “settled” merely because the Seller says so.

### 11. Do not invent consent requirements

- **Office lease:** The disclosed provision is a notification obligation, not an established landlord-consent requirement. Verify and require timely compliant notice.
- **Mossvale:** A restriction on assignment does not itself require consent to a share sale. Check the complete agreement for change-control or deemed-assignment wording before demanding consent.

These points warrant verification, not unsupported completion conditions.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Fix the liability architecture first:** prevent general limitations, disclosure and knowledge provisions from overriding bespoke protections.
2. **Protect the acquisition at Completion:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment and releases, verified share title and resolution of critical Ironquay rights.
3. **Correct the economics:** properly allocate debt, bonuses and on-costs; assess renewals without automatic deductions or double counting.
4. **Ring-fence unresolved historic risks:** targeted Ironquay and incident indemnities, separate tax protection, and suitable security for recovery.
5. **Verify the underlying record:** obtain the complete SPA, relevant contracts, funds flow and current DD evidence. The 22 September disclosure cut-off needs updating for signing and Completion, without automatically accepting new disclosures.
